intro:
Haggai, the tenth of The Twelve (Minor Prophets), ministers in 520 BC, after the exile, to the returned community in Jerusalem. Problem: People have built nice houses for themselves but God's temple remains ruins. Haggai delivers four messages in four months.

First message (ch 1): 'Is it time for you to be living in paneled houses while this house remains ruined?' Result: Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest lead rebuilding.

Second message (ch 2:1-9): To those discouraged because new temple looks small compared to Solomon's: 'The glory of this present house will be greater than the former... I will shake all nations, desired of all nations will come.'

Third message (ch 2:10-19): Through priests, explains why their crops failed: ritual impurity from neglecting temple affects everything.

Fourth message (ch 2:20-23): To Zerubbabel: 'I will make you like my signet ring'—Davidic line promise renewed.

Haggai is practical, short, effective. The people obey, temple completed in 516 BC.
outro:
Haggai addresses post-exile apathy: returning Jews prioritized comfort over worship. His message: put God's house first, and blessing follows. Not prosperity gospel but proper priorities.

The 'shake all nations' prophecy has eschatological dimension, referenced in Hebrews 12 as pointing to Christ's kingdom. Zerubbabel's mention continues Davidic line hope.

Haggai's effectiveness: people listened and acted. Shows leadership through clear, convicting messages. The book illustrates how physical rebuilding relates to spiritual revival.

Modern application: Assessing our priorities—what 'houses' are we building while God's work waits?
